    Chapter 17

    Advanced and Emerging Cryptography

    🤔 A machine that doesn’t fully exist yet already threatens secrets you send today. Plus: how to prove you know a secret without revealing a single bit of it.

    • ⏱️ ~10 min
    • 📚 7 sections
    • 🎮 5 interactive
    • ⭐ 240 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    This chapter covers ideas that sound like magic: protecting against computers that don't exist yet, proving things without revealing them, and computing on data you can't see.

    17.1Post-quantum cryptography#

    What quantum computers change

    Ordinary computers use bits (0 or 1). Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in a blend of 0 and 1 at the same time (superposition), and can be linked together (entanglement). Quantum algorithms use these effects to make wrong answers cancel out and right answers reinforce each other.

    Quantum computers are not faster at everything. But for a few specific problems, they're dramatically faster, and two of those problems matter enormously for cryptography:

    Quantum algorithm What it does Impact
    Shor's algorithm (1994) Factors numbers and solves discrete logarithms efficiently Breaks RSA, Diffie-Hellman and all elliptic-curve crypto (ECDH, ECDSA, Ed25519, X25519)
    Grover's algorithm (1996) Speeds up brute-force search (roughly square-root of the work) Weakens symmetric keys and hashes: AES-128 drops to roughly 64-bit strength in theory. AES-256 stays very strong.
    Algorithm Against a large quantum computer
    RSA, DH, ECDH, ECDSA, Ed25519, X25519 ❌ Broken
    AES-128 ⚠️ Weakened (still likely fine in practice, since Grover's algorithm is very slow to run)
    AES-256, ChaCha20 ✅ Fine
    SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-3 ✅ Fine

    When? Nobody knows. Today's quantum computers have at most a few thousand noisy, error-prone qubits, far from enough. Breaking RSA-2048 needs a large machine with error correction. Estimates have been falling: a 2025 study estimated that it could be done with under a million noisy qubits running for about a week. Many experts consider a cryptographically relevant quantum computer possible within the next 10 to 20 years.

    Harvest now, decrypt later

    Here's why this matters today: an adversary can record encrypted traffic now and store it until a quantum computer exists. Secrets that need to stay secret for 10+ years (medical records, state secrets, trade secrets, personal messages) are already at risk.

    A simple rule of thumb, known as Mosca's inequality:

    The new standards

    In 2016, NIST started a public competition, much like the one that produced AES. Teams around the world submitted 82 algorithms; cryptographers attacked them for years (several were broken along the way). In August 2024, NIST published the first standards:

    Standard Old name Type Based on Use
    FIPS 203: ML-KEM CRYSTALS-Kyber Key encapsulation (KEM) Lattices Key exchange (replaces ECDH)
    FIPS 204: ML-DSA CRYSTALS-Dilithium Signature Lattices General-purpose signatures
    FIPS 205: SLH-DSA SPHINCS+ Signature Hash functions only Conservative backup signatures
    FN-DSA (coming) Falcon Signature Lattices Compact signatures
    HQC (selected 2025) — KEM Error-correcting codes Backup KEM with different math

    The intuition behind lattice cryptography

    Most post-quantum algorithms rely on a problem called Learning With Errors (LWE). In school algebra, you solve systems of equations easily:

    Add a tiny bit of random noise to each answer, use "clock math" (mod q), and use hundreds of unknowns instead of two, and finding the secret values becomes a needle in a haystack with hundreds of dimensions. The secret is like a point hidden inside a gigantic, fuzzy multi-dimensional grid (a lattice). No known algorithm, classical or quantum, can find it efficiently.

    Hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA) are even more conservative: their security depends only on hash functions like SHA-256 being secure, which is about the most trusted assumption in cryptography. The price is large signatures.

    The trade-off: bigger keys and signatures

    Algorithm Public key Ciphertext or signature
    X25519 (classical key exchange) 32 bytes 32 bytes
    ML-KEM-768 1,184 bytes 1,088 bytes
    Ed25519 (classical signature) 32 bytes 64 bytes
    ML-DSA-65 1,952 bytes 3,309 bytes
    SLH-DSA-128s 32 bytes 7,856 bytes

    These sizes are manageable for key exchange, which is why it's been deployed first. Signatures, especially the several signatures in every certificate chain, are harder, and work on post-quantum certificates for the web is ongoing.

    Where the migration stands

    Area Status
    HTTPS key exchange ✅ Hybrid X25519MLKEM768 is the default in major browsers, Cloudflare and OpenSSL 3.5+
    SSH ✅ OpenSSH 10 uses mlkem768x25519-sha256 by default
    Messaging ✅ Signal (PQXDH and a post-quantum ratchet), iMessage (PQ3)
    Certificates and signatures 🔄 In progress
    Government timelines NIST has proposed deprecating today's quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms around 2030 and disallowing them by 2035. The US NSA's "CNSA 2.0" sets similar deadlines for national-security systems.

    💡 Key idea: crypto agility. The PQ migration shows why systems should be designed so algorithms can be swapped without rebuilding everything. The next migration will come too.

    Quantum key distribution (QKD): a different idea

    Don't confuse post-quantum cryptography (new math that runs on normal computers) with quantum key distribution, which uses physics. QKD sends single particles of light (photons) over special fiber links. Measuring a photon disturbs it, so an eavesdropper creates detectable errors (the BB84 protocol, 1984). It needs dedicated hardware, works only over limited distances, and still needs classical authentication. Most security agencies recommend post-quantum cryptography rather than QKD for general use.

    FIPS 203, lattices

    ML-DSA (Dilithium)

    SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)

    FIPS 205, hashes only

    FN-DSA (Falcon)

    Compact lattice signatures

    • Small signatures
    • Tricky floating-point implementation

    👍 Situational
    HQC

    Code-based KEM, selected 2025

    QKD

    Quantum key distribution

    • Security from physics
    • Special hardware and fiber; short range
    • Still needs authentication
    • Not recommended by most agencies
    Best for: Niche experiments

    17.2Zero-knowledge proofs: proving without revealing#

    A zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) lets you prove a statement is true without revealing anything else. For example: proving you know a password without revealing it, or proving you're over 18 without revealing your birthday.

    The cave story. A cave has a ring-shaped tunnel with a magic door in the middle that opens only with a secret word.

    1. Peggy (the prover) goes into the cave and picks path A or B at random, while Victor (the verifier) waits outside.
    2. Victor walks to the entrance and shouts: "Come out of path A!" (or B, at random).
    3. If Peggy knows the word, she can always come out of the requested path, opening the door if needed.
    4. If she doesn't, she has a 50% chance of having picked the right path by luck.

    Repeat 20 times. A faker would have to be lucky every time: a 1 in 1,048,576 chance. Victor becomes convinced Peggy knows the word, yet he learns nothing about the word itself. He also can't convince anyone else, since a video of the exchange could have been staged.

    Another analogy: to prove you've found Waldo in a "Where's Waldo?" picture without revealing where he is, cover the page with a huge sheet of cardboard that has a small hole, and position it so only Waldo shows through.

    Real uses:

    • Privacy cryptocurrencies (Zcash) prove a transaction is valid without revealing amounts or parties.
    • Blockchain scaling ("zk-rollups") prove that thousands of transactions were processed correctly with one small proof.
    • Digital identity: prove "I'm over 18" or "I live in this country" from a digital ID without revealing your name or birth date. Digital ID wallets in the EU and elsewhere are adopting this.
    • You'll see acronyms like zk-SNARK and zk-STARK, which are families of efficient zero-knowledge proof systems.

    Zero-knowledge proofs

    💡 Concept
    zk-SNARKs

    Succinct proofs

    • Tiny proofs, fast verification

    • Heavy to generate
    Best for: Blockchain privacy and scaling
    💡 Concept
    zk-STARKs

    Transparent proofs

    • No trusted setup; hash-based (post-quantum)
    • Bigger proofs
    Best for: Rollups

    17.3Homomorphic encryption: computing on locked data#

    Homomorphic encryption lets someone perform calculations on encrypted data without decrypting it. The result, once decrypted by the owner, is the answer to the calculation.

    Analogy: the jeweler's glovebox. A jewelry-shop owner wants workers to assemble necklaces from gold without letting them pocket any. She puts the gold in a locked, transparent box with gloves built into the sides. Workers can assemble the necklace inside, but can't take anything out. Only the owner, with the key, opens the box.

    You've already seen a tiny homomorphic property. Remember that textbook RSA is "malleable"? Multiplying two RSA ciphertexts multiplies the hidden messages:

    Python
    n, e, d = 3233, 17, 2753                 # toy RSA keys from Chapter 9
enc = lambda m: pow(m, e, n)
dec = lambda c: pow(c, d, n)

c2, c3 = enc(2), enc(3)                  # 1752 and 1211: meaningless to an observer
product = (c2 * c3) % n                  # someone multiplies the CIPHERTEXTS
print(dec(product))                      # 6  = 2 × 3, computed without seeing 2 or 3
    Type What you can compute Example
    Partially homomorphic One operation only (multiply, or add) RSA (multiply), Paillier (add, used in some e-voting systems)
    Fully homomorphic (FHE) Any computation First built by Craig Gentry in 2009

    FHE is still much slower than normal computation (often thousands of times or more), but it's improving fast and is starting to appear in real products: for example, services that look something up on your behalf (a caller ID, a landmark in a photo) without learning what you asked about. Apple has used homomorphic encryption for features like this.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Homomorphic encryption

    💡 Concept
    Partially homomorphic

    One operation (RSA ×, Paillier +)

    • Fast and practical today
    • Only one kind of math
    Best for: E-voting tallies, simple sums
    💡 Concept
    Fully homomorphic (FHE)

    Any computation on ciphertext

    • Cloud can compute without seeing data
    • Thousands to millions of times slower
    • Huge ciphertexts
    Best for: Specialized private analytics

    17.4Secret sharing: splitting a key among people#

    What if a key is so important that no single person should be able to use it, but losing one person shouldn't lose the key either? Shamir's Secret Sharing (Adi Shamir, 1979) splits a secret into n shares so that any k of them can rebuild it, and fewer than k reveal nothing at all.

    The intuition: two points define a line.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python, "any 3 of 5"):

    Python
    import secrets
PRIME = 2**127 - 1          # all arithmetic is "clock math" modulo a large prime

def make_shares(secret, threshold, count):
    # random polynomial: f(x) = secret + a1*x + a2*x^2 + ... ; f(0) = secret
    coeffs = [secret] + [secrets.randbelow(PRIME) for _ in range(threshold - 1)]
    f = lambda x: sum(c * pow(x, i, PRIME) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % PRIME
    return [(x, f(x)) for x in range(1, count + 1)]

def recover(shares):
    # Lagrange interpolation: rebuild the curve and read off f(0)
    total = 0
    for i, (xi, yi) in enumerate(shares):
        num, den = 1, 1
        for j, (xj, _) in enumerate(shares):
            if i != j:
                num = num * (-xj) % PRIME
                den = den * (xi - xj) % PRIME
        total = (total + yi * num * pow(den, -1, PRIME)) % PRIME
    return total

shares = make_shares(123456789, threshold=3, count=5)
print(recover(shares[:3]))                          # 123456789
print(recover([shares[0], shares[2], shares[4]]))   # 123456789 (any 3 work)
print(recover(shares[:2]))                          # garbage: 2 shares aren't enough

    Real uses:

    • Certificate authority and DNSSEC root keys: the DNS root key's backup is split among trusted people around the world, a certain number of whom must come together to restore it. (This is the true story behind headlines about "seven people who hold the keys to the internet.")
    • Unsealing secret managers: HashiCorp Vault, by default, needs several key holders to unlock it after a restart.
    • Cryptocurrency wallet backups and company "break-glass" master passwords.
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Splitting secrets

    ✅ Use it
    Shamir secret sharing

    Any k of n shares

    • Fewer than k shares reveal nothing
    • Survives losing up to n − k shares
    • Secret is rebuilt in one place (a moment of exposure)
    • Shares need secure storage
    Best for: Root-key backups, Vault unsealing
    ❌ Avoid
    Single key holder

    One person, one key

    • Simple
    • Single point of failure and of corruption
    Best for: Low-value secrets only
    ✔ section read

    17.5Multi-party computation and threshold signatures#

    Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets several people jointly compute a result from their private inputs while learning only the result.

    The classic example is Yao's Millionaires' Problem (1982): two millionaires want to know who is richer without either revealing their wealth.

    A simpler example you can run: three colleagues want their average salary without anyone revealing their own. Each splits their salary into three random-looking pieces that add up to it, keeps one, and hands one to each colleague. Each person adds up the pieces they hold and announces only that sum. The three sums add up to the total, but no individual salary is ever revealed:

    Python
    import secrets
M = 2**64                                    # clock math so pieces look random
salaries = {"Ana": 72000, "Ben": 58000, "Chen": 91000}

pieces = {}
for person, salary in salaries.items():
    r1, r2 = secrets.randbelow(M), secrets.randbelow(M)
    pieces[person] = [r1, r2, (salary - r1 - r2) % M]   # three random pieces summing to salary

# Person i receives piece i from everyone and announces only the sum
announced = [sum(pieces[p][i] for p in salaries) % M for i in range(3)]
total = sum(announced) % M
print(total, total / 3)                      # 221000  73666.67  (nobody's salary revealed)

    Real uses:

    • Threshold signatures: a signing key is split among several servers or devices, and a signature requires several of them to cooperate. The full private key never exists in one place. Used by cryptocurrency custody providers ("MPC wallets") and some certificate and key-management systems.
    • Private set intersection: two parties find what they have in common (for example, which of your contacts use an app) without revealing the rest of their lists.
    • Privacy-preserving statistics and advertising measurement.
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Distributed key use

    💡 Concept
    MPC

    Compute jointly, reveal only the result

    • No party sees others’ inputs
    • Network-heavy; complex
    Best for: Private auctions, statistics
    ✅ Use it
    Threshold signatures

    The key is never in one place

    • No single device can sign alone
    • Looks like one normal signature
    • Complex protocols; fewer audited libraries
    Best for: Custody wallets, CAs
    ✔ section read

    17.6PAKE: secure key exchange from a password#

    A PAKE (Password-Authenticated Key Exchange) lets two parties who share only a password (possibly a weak one) create a strong shared key, in a way that:

    • an eavesdropper learns nothing, and
    • even a man-in-the-middle gets only one guess per attempt, with no way to test passwords offline.

    You've already met one: SAE in WPA3 Wi-Fi (Chapter 15). Others include SRP (used in Apple's iCloud Keychain recovery) and OPAQUE, a modern design in which the server never sees the password at all, even during registration.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    PAKE

    ✅ Use it
    PAKE (OPAQUE, SRP, SAE)

    Key exchange from a password

    • No offline guessing from traffic
    • Server never sees the password (OPAQUE)
    • Harder to deploy than password-over-TLS
    Best for: Wi-Fi (WPA3), password managers
    ✔ section read

    17.7Other ideas worth knowing#

    Idea Plain description Where it's used
    Commitment scheme Like a sealed envelope: commit to a value now, reveal it later, and you can't change it in between Fair coin flips online, sealed-bid auctions, inside ZK proofs
    Blind signature Get something signed without the signer seeing what it is David Chaum's digital cash (1982); "Privacy Pass" tokens that let you skip CAPTCHAs without being tracked
    Ring / group signature Prove "someone in this group signed" without revealing who Monero; anonymous credentials
    Format-preserving encryption Encrypt a 16-digit card number into another 16-digit number Payment systems, legacy databases
    Searchable encryption Search encrypted data without decrypting it Encrypted databases
    Key transparency A public, auditable log of users' public keys so a messaging service can't secretly swap them WhatsApp, iMessage Contact Key Verification
    Confidential computing Hardware-isolated "enclaves" that keep data encrypted in memory, even from the cloud provider Intel TDX, AMD SEV, Apple Private Cloud Compute
